\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

The central result is that persuasion-aware fine-tuning bridges the cross-attack generalization gap that vanilla semantic temporal modeling cannot: DisPeD achieves F1 = 1.000 on unseen Deceptive Delight conversations, a +72 percentage point improvement over vanilla DeBERTa (F1 = 0.284), with zero degradation under adversarial paraphrasing.
Ablation experiments isolate the mechanism behind this gain.
Scrambled persuasion strategy labels reduce OOD F1 by only 1 percentage point, and replacing BiGRU with mean pooling yields identical performance.
These results establish that fine-tuning on persuasion-related text, not specific label assignments or temporal modeling, is the critical ingredient.
The encoder functions as a persuasion-presence detector: exposure to persuasion-domain conversations during multi-task training teaches it to attend to pragmatic cues that transfer across attack families, regardless of supervision quality.
Binary fine-tuning on persuasion-domain text without the strategy classification head also achieves competitive detection performance, confirming that domain exposure drives the generalization gain.
LLM-as-judge baselines confirm the insufficiency of content-level reasoning: GPT-5.5 achieves F1 of only 0.191 to 0.449 on in-distribution Crescendo detection, with 30 to 47\% of responses unparseable.
The 9-class taxonomy is retained not for detection accuracy but for interpretability: distinct attack types produce recognizable persuasion signatures in strategy trajectory analysis that security analysts can inspect without post-hoc explanation methods.

First, the dataset is small: 500 training conversations and 160 OOD test conversations.
These results require validation at larger scale before deployment claims are warranted.
Second, all conversations were generated by Qwen3-8B; real-world multi-turn attacks authored by human adversaries may exhibit different characteristics that our synthetic data does not capture.
Third, DisPeD detects persuasion presence per turn rather than temporal trajectories, so attacks that distribute persuasion sparsely across many turns might evade the detector.

Each intermediate turn is indistinguishable from a legitimate query. Representation engineering analyses confirm that individual attack turns occupy the same embedding region as genuinely benign text in pretrained encoders~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}, rendering per-turn safety filters ineffective. The common mechanism underlying these attacks is \emph{persuasion}: each attack type implements a distinct but systematic strategy for manipulating the model's compliance over multiple conversational exchanges~\citep{li2024mhj}. Detecting these attacks therefore requires moving beyond content-level analysis to capture the pragmatic dynamics of the conversation.
7	
8	Current defenses fail to address this challenge along two axes: granularity and representation. Production safety classifiers such as Llama Guard~\citep{inan2023llamaguard}, WildGuard~\citep{han2024wildguard}, and ShieldGemma~\citep{zeng2024shieldgemma} operate on individual turns and cannot model manipulation trajectories that unfold across multiple exchanges. These systems are designed to detect overtly harmful content in isolation and are fundamentally blind to the distributed nature of multi-turn attacks, where the adversarial intent only becomes apparent through the cumulative progression of turns. The natural alternative is to encode full conversations with a pretrained language model and track semantic drift over turns. This approach, exemplified by temporal aggregation over generic embeddings (the ``DeepContext'' paradigm~\citep{deepcontext2026}), performs well when the test distribution matches training: all methods we evaluate, including bag-of-words baselines, achieve near-perfect F1 on in-distribution Crescendo conversations. The critical failure emerges on unseen attack types. A vanilla DeBERTa encoder with the same temporal aggregation pipeline collapses from F1 = 1.000 on in-distribution data to F1 = 0.284 on out-of-distribution (OOD) Deceptive Delight conversations. This collapse worsens as more turns are observed (F1 drops from 0.575 at turn 1 to 0.284 on the full conversation), consistent with the finding that each additional attack turn supplies misleading ``benign'' evidence to the generic encoder~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}. LLM-as-judge approaches fare no better: GPT-5.5 achieves F1 of only 0.191 to 0.449 on Crescendo detection, with 30 to 47\% of responses unparseable, confirming that content-level reasoning cannot detect adversarial intent distributed across benign turns. The gap is clear: no existing method uses persuasion-grounded representations, and methods that rely on surface semantics or content-level reasoning fail to generalize across attack families.
9	
10	The key observation motivating our approach is that persuasion in jailbreak attacks is both \emph{systematic} and \emph{extractable}. \citet{zeng2024pap} identify 40 persuasion techniques across jailbreak attacks through their Persuasion Attack Paradigm (PAP), and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} find identifiable persuasion strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. These findings establish that multi-turn attacks are not ad hoc manipulation but structured persuasion campaigns that follow recognizable patterns. On the extraction side, recent work on LLM persuasion demonstrates that these pragmatic dynamics leave detectable traces in turn-level representations~\citep{jaipersaud2025howdollmspersuade}, and that the persuasion literature offers well-established taxonomies (e.g., Cialdini's six principles of influence~\citep{cialdini2001influence}) to categorize these strategies. The resulting representations would capture the functional structure of manipulation, a structure shared across attack types regardless of their surface realization. The gap is clear: no existing method uses persuasion-grounded representations, and methods that rely on surface semantics or content-level reasoning fail to generalize across attack families.

The key observation motivating our approach is that persuasion in jailbreak attacks is both \emph{systematic} and \emph{extractable}. \citet{zeng2024pap} identify 40 persuasion techniques across jailbreak attacks through their Persuasion Attack Paradigm (PAP), and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} find identifiable persuasion strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. These findings establish that multi-turn attacks are not ad hoc manipulation but structured persuasion campaigns that follow recognizable patterns. On the extraction side, recent work on LLM persuasion demonstrates that these pragmatic dynamics leave detectable traces in turn-level representations~\citep{jaipersaud2025howdollmspersuade}, and that the persuasion literature offers well-established taxonomies (e.g., Cialdini's six principles of influence~\citep{cialdini2001influence}) to categorize these strategies. If persuasion is systematic (attacks follow identifiable strategy patterns) and extractable (representations can encode these patterns), then fine-tuning an encoder on persuasion-related text should teach it to attend to pragmatic features rather than topical content. The resulting representations would capture the functional structure of manipulation, a structure shared across attack types regardless of their surface realization. This is not a new theoretical claim but an operationalization of observations already established in the literature: our contribution is to demonstrate that this operationalization produces measurable gains in cross-attack generalization.

We propose \textbf{DisPeD} (Discourse-level Persuasion Detection), a two-stage framework that implements this idea. In Stage~1, we fine-tune a DeBERTa-v3-base encoder~\citep{he2021deberta} with a multi-task objective that combines 9-class persuasion strategy classification and binary jailbreak-intent classification at the turn level. The 9-class taxonomy is grounded in PAP~\citep{zeng2024pap} and Cialdini's principles of influence~\citep{cialdini2001influence}, covering strategies from rapport building and authority appeal to gradual escalation and direct request. The persuasion classification task forces the encoder to learn representations that distinguish between pragmatic strategies, while the intent task anchors these representations to the detection objective. In Stage~2, we aggregate turn-level [CLS] embeddings via a bidirectional GRU (BiGRU) and train a lightweight MLP for conversation-level binary classification. The full architecture is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}. The design is deliberately simple: the ablation study (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that replacing BiGRU with orderless mean pooling yields identical performance, and that even scrambled persuasion labels reduce OOD detection by only 1 percentage point relative to the full taxonomy, while vanilla DeBERTa without fine-tuning trails by over 70 percentage points. The fine-tuning process on persuasion-related text, not label accuracy or temporal modeling, is the critical ingredient for cross-attack generalization. This finding indicates that exposure to in-domain text reshapes the encoder's feature space even when the supervision signal is noisy or coarse. In our setting, multi-task training on persuasion-annotated conversations teaches the encoder to attend to pragmatic cues (implicit requests, escalation markers, rapport-building patterns) that transfer across attack families.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=4pt]
  \item \textbf{Cross-attack generalization through persuasion-aware fine-tuning.} DisPeD achieves F1 = 1.000 on unseen Deceptive Delight conversations, a +72 percentage point improvement over vanilla DeBERTa (F1 = 0.284) trained on the same Crescendo data. Ablation experiments show that scrambled strategy labels reduce OOD F1 by only 1 percentage point, confirming that fine-tuning on persuasion-domain text is the mechanism that bridges the cross-attack generalization gap (Section~\ref{sec:cross_attack}, Section~\ref{sec:ablation}).

  \item \textbf{Interpretable detection through persuasion strategy trajectories.} The 9-class persuasion taxonomy provides native interpretability: different attack types exhibit distinct strategy signatures that security analysts can inspect. Crescendo exhibits broad transition coverage across all strategy categories; FITD concentrates transitions in 4 active strategies with a dominant role-assignment-to-obfuscation pattern. These trajectories explain detection decisions without requiring post-hoc interpretability methods (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}).

  \item \textbf{Robustness to adversarial perturbation.} DisPeD maintains zero degradation (0 percentage points) under adversarial paraphrasing, while vanilla DeBERTa degrades by 11.8 percentage points and TF-IDF by 1.3 percentage points. Combined with cross-attack robustness, this confirms that persuasion-aware representations are invariant to both surface variation and attack-type shift (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
\end{itemize}

Persuasion-aware fine-tuning enables robust detection of unseen attack types where vanilla semantic embeddings collapse.
Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents F1 scores across three test conditions: IID Crescendo, OOD Deceptive Delight, and OOD FITD.
Figure~\ref{fig:cross_attack} provides a visual comparison at full conversation length.

\paragraph{IID performance.}
All three methods achieve near-perfect F1 on in-distribution Crescendo test data.
TF-IDF LR and DisPeD both reach F1 = 1.000 at every prefix length, and Vanilla DeBERTa ranges from 0.968 to 1.000.
This ceiling effect reflects an inherent lexical separability between persuasive jailbreak and general benign conversations: even bag-of-words features suffice when the test distribution matches training.
The IID results confirm that persuasion-aware fine-tuning does not sacrifice in-distribution accuracy.
Vanilla DeBERTa shows the most variance at early prefixes ($K$=1: std=0.033), where fewer turns provide less signal for generic embeddings.
DisPeD achieves zero variance (std=0.000) across all prefix lengths, reflecting stable representations even with limited context.

\paragraph{OOD: Deceptive Delight.}
The DD evaluation reveals the central finding of this paper.
Vanilla DeBERTa, the natural approach of encoding turns with a generic pretrained model, collapses to F1 = 0.284 on full DD conversations despite reaching 1.000 on IID data from the same pipeline.
The degradation worsens as more turns are observed: F1 drops from 0.575 at $K$=1 to 0.284 at Full.
This counterintuitive pattern is consistent with prior work showing that multi-turn attack turns are designed to remain in a ``benign'' embedding region~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}: each additional DD turn supplies more misleading ``benign'' evidence, pushing the model toward incorrect predictions rather than helping it detect the attack.
DisPeD maintains F1 $\geq$ 0.990 at every prefix length, including near-perfect early detection at $K$=1 (F1 = 1.000) and $K$=2 (F1 = 0.990).
The gap over Vanilla DeBERTa ranges from +42 percentage points at $K$=1 to +72 percentage points at Full.
Early detection is particularly important for deployment: at $K$=2, DisPeD detects attacks after just two turns (F1 = 0.990) while Vanilla DeBERTa has already dropped to 0.438.

TF-IDF LR achieves F1 = 0.944 on full DD conversations, which confirms substantial lexical separability even across attack families.
We acknowledge this result openly: the primary contribution of DisPeD over TF-IDF is not raw detection performance but rather three complementary advantages.
First, DisPeD bridges the representation-level gap that vanilla semantic embeddings cannot (+72 percentage points on DD), validating persuasion-aware fine-tuning as the mechanism for cross-attack generalization.
Second, DisPeD achieves zero degradation under adversarial perturbation (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
Third, DisPeD provides interpretable strategy trajectories for detection decisions (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}).

\paragraph{OOD: FITD.}
FITD conversations are easier to detect across all methods.
DisPeD and Vanilla DeBERTa both reach F1 $\geq$ 0.990 at all evaluated prefixes, and TF-IDF LR achieves 1.000 on $K$=1 and full conversations.
The limited differentiation on FITD suggests this attack family shares more surface-level features with the Crescendo training data than DD does, reducing the cross-attack generalization challenge.

\label{sec:ablation}

\centering
\small
\caption{Ablation study on OOD Deceptive Delight and IID. All variants trained on Crescendo. The persuasion fine-tuning process is the critical factor; label granularity and temporal modeling are not.}

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The fine-tuning process on persuasion-related text, not specific label assignments, is what drives cross-attack generalization.
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports DD-OOD and IID F1 for several model variants, grouped into fine-tuned variants (above the mid-rule) and the unfine-tuned baseline (below).

\paragraph{Label granularity.}
Replacing the 9-class persuasion taxonomy with randomly scrambled labels reduces DD-Full F1 from 1.000 to 0.990, a gap of just 1 percentage point.
Collapsing the taxonomy to binary (persuasion-present vs.\ absent) yields the same 0.990.
Both variants remain far above the vanilla baseline (F1 = 0.284), a gap exceeding 70 percentage points.
These results confirm that the encoder learns useful pragmatic features from exposure to persuasion-domain text during fine-tuning, regardless of whether strategy labels are correct, coarse, or random.
The data domain matters more than the specific supervision signal~\citep{gururangan2020dontstop}.
In our setting, multi-task fine-tuning on persuasion-related conversations teaches the encoder to attend to pragmatic features (e.g., implicit requests, escalation cues, rapport-building patterns) that transfer across attack types.
The 9-class taxonomy provides interpretability through strategy trajectory analysis (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}) rather than a detection advantage over coarser alternatives.
From a practical standpoint, this result lowers the annotation barrier: coarse or imperfect persuasion labels suffice for training an effective cross-attack detector.

\paragraph{Temporal modeling.}
Replacing BiGRU with orderless mean pooling over the [CLS] sequence yields DD-Full F1 = 1.000, matching the BiGRU default.
This equivalence confirms that the model detects persuasion presence in individual turns rather than relying on the temporal ordering of strategies across the conversation.
BiGRU is the default aggregator in all other experiments.

\paragraph{Fine-tuning as the critical factor.}
The most informative comparison spans all ablation rows.
Every variant that includes persuasion-domain fine-tuning achieves DD-Full F1 $\geq$ 0.990, while Vanilla DeBERTa collapses to 0.284.
All fine-tuned variants also maintain IID-Full F1 = 1.000.
This 70+ percentage point gap on OOD data establishes that persuasion-aware fine-tuning is both necessary and sufficient for cross-attack generalization; architecture choices and label granularity are secondary factors.
We also evaluated an $\alpha=0$ variant (persuasion strategy classification only, no intent task), which achieves IID-Full F1 = 1.000. OOD evaluation was not conducted for this variant, but the IID result confirms that the persuasion task alone suffices for in-distribution detection. The intent head provides a complementary training signal but is not required when the persuasion task drives representation learning.

\paragraph{Domain-adaptive controls.}
The scrambled-label result raises a question: does the encoder benefit from persuasion-specific pragmatic features, or from domain adaptation on conversational text more broadly? To isolate this, we are conducting two control experiments. The first replaces the persuasion strategy head with sentiment classification on the same training data, testing whether any auxiliary task on in-domain text suffices. The second applies masked language modeling (MLM) on the training conversations without any classification head, testing whether unsupervised domain adaptation alone accounts for the OOD gains. \texttt{[PENDING: plan\_016/017 domain-adaptive control results]}

\label{sec:perturbation}

\label{tab:perturbation}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & Original & Perturbed & $\Delta$ (pp) \\

DisPeD maintains perfect detection under adversarial paraphrasing while both baselines degrade.
Table~\ref{tab:perturbation} reports F1 on the original and perturbed IID test sets (76 samples each).
The perturbed set was constructed via automated paraphrasing that preserves semantic content (BERTScore 0.92) while substantially altering surface forms (lexical overlap 0.20).

DisPeD achieves F1 = 1.000 on both original and perturbed data, with zero degradation.
Vanilla DeBERTa drops from 1.000 to 0.882, a loss of 11.8 percentage points, consistent with its reliance on surface-level features from the unfine-tuned encoder.
TF-IDF LR shows a smaller but measurable decline from 1.000 to 0.987 (1.3 percentage points).
The ordering follows the expected robustness hierarchy: features learned through persuasion-aware fine-tuning capture pragmatic patterns that are invariant to surface rephrasing, while generic embeddings and lexical features are more sensitive to word-level changes.
Combined with the cross-attack results in Table~\ref{tab:main_results}, the perturbation evaluation confirms that persuasion-aware fine-tuning produces representations robust to both unseen attack types and adversarial surface variation.
The zero-degradation result is particularly relevant for deployment scenarios where attackers may attempt to evade detection through paraphrasing or style transfer~\citep{nasr2025attackermovessecond}.
While our perturbation evaluation uses automated paraphrasing rather than adversary-crafted evasion, the 11.8 percentage point degradation of Vanilla DeBERTa under even this moderate perturbation suggests that unfine-tuned representations would be fragile against more targeted adaptive attacks.

\subsection{LLM-as-Judge Baseline}
\label{sec:llm_judge}

\centering
\small
\caption{LLM-as-judge zero-shot Crescendo detection (IID test set). F1 values exclude unparseable responses and therefore represent upper bounds.$^{\dagger}$Unparseable rate increases with context length: 30\% at $K$=2 to 47\% at Full.}
\label{tab:llm_judge}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & $K$=2 & $K$=3 & $K$=5 & Full & Unparse. \\
\midrule
GPT-5.5 & .191 & .273 & .449 & .383 & 30--47\%$^{\dagger}$ \\
Qwen3-8B & .000 & .051 & .146 & .100 & 0\% \\
\midrule
DisPeD (ours) & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & 0\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Frontier language models fail at multi-turn jailbreak detection even when given full conversation context.
Table~\ref{tab:llm_judge} reports zero-shot detection performance for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3-8B on the IID Crescendo test set, where both models are prompted to classify each conversation as jailbreak or benign.

GPT-5.5 achieves precision of 1.0 at all turn prefixes but recall ranges from only 0.105 to 0.290, resulting in F1 of 0.191 at $K$=2 and 0.449 at $K$=5.
A substantial fraction of GPT-5.5 responses are unparseable: the rate increases from 30\% at $K$=2 to 47\% on full conversations.
The F1 values in Table~\ref{tab:llm_judge} exclude unparseable responses and therefore represent upper bounds on actual performance.
Full-conversation F1 (0.383) is lower than $K$=5 F1 (0.449) because the unparseable rate grows with context length, not because the model classifies worse on parsed responses.
The high precision but low recall pattern suggests that GPT-5.5 is deceived by Crescendo's surface educational framing: when the model does commit to a classification, it correctly identifies jailbreaks, but the majority of attacks go undetected.

Qwen3-8B performs worse across all prefixes, with F1 from 0.000 at $K$=2 to 0.100 on full conversations, and produces no unparseable responses.
The failure of both a frontier commercial model and an open-weight model highlights a fundamental limitation of content-level reasoning for this task.
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo,li2024mhj}, and each turn maintains surface-level coherence with an innocuous cover topic.
An LLM analyzing conversation content sees a plausible discussion and lacks the pragmatic signal to recognize the underlying persuasion process.
DisPeD's learned persuasion features capture this pragmatic layer at a fraction of the inference cost of a frontier LLM, without requiring the conversation content to contain explicit harmful requests.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Strategy Trajectory Analysis}
\label{sec:strategy}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/paper/fig3_strategy_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Persuasion strategy transition count matrices for three attack types, based on ground-truth intended strategy labels from the dataset generation pipeline. Color intensity reflects transition count on a symmetric log scale; white cells indicate zero transitions. Crescendo exhibits broad coverage across all strategy categories, while FITD and DD concentrate transitions in smaller subsets.}
\label{fig:strategy_heatmap}
\end{figure*}

Different multi-turn attack types produce distinct persuasion strategy transition patterns that provide native interpretability for detection decisions.
Figure~\ref{fig:strategy_heatmap} shows transition count matrices based on ground-truth intended strategy labels for three attack types.

Crescendo conversations exhibit broad transition coverage across all strategy categories, with 1,818 total transitions.
The highest concentration appears in Role Assignment self-transitions (545), with substantial activity across Emotional Manipulation, Logical Reframing, and Authority Appeal transitions.
This diverse pattern reflects Crescendo's design: each turn draws from a wide repertoire of strategies while incrementally shifting toward more aggressive persuasion.

FITD conversations show a markedly sparser pattern with 541 transitions concentrated in 4 active source strategies.
Role$\to$Obfuscation (161) is the dominant transition, consistent with FITD's structure of securing initial compliance through role assignment before obscuring the escalation path.

DD conversations span 5 active source strategies across 565 transitions.
Emotion$\to$Obfuscation (129) is the dominant transition, consistent with DD's hybrid design of embedding harmful content within emotionally engaging and distracting contexts~\citep{deceptivedelight2024}.

These trajectory signatures serve two purposes.
For practitioners, they provide human-interpretable explanations for detection decisions: a security analyst can inspect the strategy sequence to understand why a conversation was flagged.
For the research question, the diversity of trajectories across attack families confirms that persuasion-aware fine-tuning captures generalizable pragmatic structure rather than memorizing surface patterns from a single attack type.
We emphasize that strategy trajectories are an interpretability contribution, not a detection mechanism: the ablation in Section~\ref{sec:ablation} shows that replacing BiGRU with mean pooling (which discards turn order) yields identical performance, so DisPeD detects persuasion presence per turn rather than relying on temporal trajectory patterns.

3	\section{Related Work}
4	\label{sec:related_work}
5	
6	\subsection{Multi-Turn Jailbreak Attacks}
7	
8	Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across a sequence of individually benign conversational turns, exploiting the inability of safety systems to track manipulation over time. These attacks draw on distinct persuasion strategies: Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} implements gradual escalation, building rapport before incrementally steering the conversation toward harmful content; FITD~\citep{fitd2024} exploits commitment-consistency bias by eliciting small compliances that anchor the model before requesting forbidden output; Deceptive Delight~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} combines emotional manipulation with role assignment to bypass safety training. ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} constructs actor networks where multiple personas collaboratively steer conversations, and PAIR~\citep{chao2023pair} automates the iterative refinement of attack prompts through attacker-judge feedback loops. \citet{wei2023jailbroken} provide a taxonomy grounded in two failure modes (competing objectives and mismatched generalization), offering a unifying framework for understanding why these attacks succeed. Across this diverse landscape, a shared structural pattern emerges: successful multi-turn attacks rely on systematic persuasion dynamics~\citep{zeng2024pap,hagendorff2026reasoning,li2024mhj} rather than token-level adversarial optimization. This distinguishes them from single-turn attacks such as GCG~\citep{zou2023gcg}, where gradient-based suffix optimization operates at the token level without conversational persuasion. DisPeD specifically targets the persuasion-grounded attack family, treating their shared reliance on pragmatic manipulation as the signal for cross-attack detection.
9	
10	\subsection{Multi-Turn Defenses}
11	
12	Existing multi-turn defenses model conversation-level structure but lack grounding in the persuasion mechanisms that attacks exploit. DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026} tracks semantic drift by aggregating BERT embeddings with a recurrent network, achieving F1 = 0.84 on in-distribution conversations but failing on unseen attack types because generic embeddings encode topical content rather than pragmatic function. BIID~\citep{tong2025biid} performs intention inference at each turn to detect escalation, yet the inferred intentions remain at the semantic level and do not capture the underlying persuasion strategy. G-Guard~\citep{gguard2025} models conversations as graphs and applies GNN-based classification, and SafeDream~\citep{safedream2026} uses world-model predictions to anticipate unsafe continuations. Both approaches improve over per-turn classification but remain agnostic to why specific turn sequences constitute attacks. The common limitation is clear: none of these methods ground their representations in the persuasion structure of attacks. DisPeD addresses this gap by fine-tuning on persuasion strategy classification, producing representations that encode pragmatic dynamics and transfer across attack families without retraining.
13	
14	\subsection{Production Safety Systems}
15	
16	Deployed safety classifiers operate at the individual turn level. Llama Guard~\citep{inan2023llamaguard} and its successor Llama Guard 3~\citep{metallamaguard3_2024} classify each user input and model output against a predefined safety taxonomy. ShieldGemma~\citep{zeng2024shieldgemma} and WildGuard~\citep{han2024wildguard} similarly provide per-turn moderation with broader coverage of harm categories, and Constitutional Classifiers~\citep{anthropic2025constitutional} derive safety boundaries from red-teaming exercises. These systems excel at identifying overtly harmful content but cannot model manipulation trajectories that span multiple turns. When no single turn contains an explicit policy violation, per-turn classifiers have no signal to trigger on. LLM-as-judge approaches represent an alternative, but our experiments show that GPT-5.5 achieves F1 = 0.191 to 0.449 on multi-turn jailbreak detection, with substantial portions of responses unparseable. This confirms that content-level reasoning, even from frontier models, is insufficient when adversarial intent is distributed across benign turns. DisPeD complements these production systems by providing a conversation-level detection layer that captures the pragmatic trajectory of multi-turn interactions.
17	
18	\subsection{Discourse Analysis and Computational Persuasion}
19	
20	The analysis of pragmatic structure in dialogue has a long history. Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST)~\citep{mann1988rst} models coherence relations between text spans, the Penn Discourse TreeBank (PDTB)~\citep{prasad2008pdtb} annotates discourse connectives and implicit relations, and dialogue act taxonomies~\citep{stolcke2000dialogueact} classify utterance functions. Speech Act Theory, from \citet{austin1962speechacts} and \citet{searle1969speechacts}, distinguishes between what is literally said (locutionary acts) and what is accomplished through saying it (illocutionary acts). Existing jailbreak detectors operate at the locutionary level, classifying the surface content of turns. DisPeD targets the illocutionary level by encoding the persuasive function of each turn.
21	
22	In computational persuasion, \citet{habernal2016convincingness} model argument convincingness and \citet{tan2016winningarguments} analyze persuasion success in online debates. For jailbreak attacks specifically, PAP~\citep{zeng2024pap} identifies 40 persuasion techniques used across attack types, grounded in Cialdini's six principles of influence~\citep{cialdini2001influence} (reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity). Recent work establishes two critical facts: \citet{jaipersaud2025howdollmspersuade} show that persuasion dynamics are extractable from model representations, and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} find identifiable persuasion strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. DisPeD operationalizes these observations by using persuasion strategy classification as a fine-tuning objective, transforming the theoretical link between persuasion and jailbreaking into a practical detection mechanism.
23	
24	\subsection{Domain-Adaptive Pretraining and Multi-Task Learning}
25	
26	Domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT) improves downstream task performance by continuing pretraining on unlabeled text from the target domain before task-specific fine-tuning~\citep{gururangan2020dontstop}. \citet{gururangan2020dontstop} show that DAPT yields consistent gains across four domains (biomedical, computer science, news, reviews), with further improvements from task-adaptive pretraining on the unlabeled task data itself. Supplementary training on intermediate labeled tasks (STILTs) extends this principle by fine-tuning on a related labeled dataset before the target task~\citep{phang2018stilts}, and multi-task learning jointly optimizes across related objectives to learn shared representations~\citep{caruana1997multitask,liu2019mtdnn}.
27	
28	DisPeD's Stage-1 fine-tuning shares structural similarities with both STILTs and multi-task learning: the encoder is trained on persuasion strategy classification (an intermediate task) jointly with binary intent detection before being used for conversation-level classification. The motivation differs from standard DAPT. General DAPT adapts representations to a domain's vocabulary and distributional patterns, while DisPeD's persuasion-aware fine-tuning targets a specific pragmatic capability, distinguishing persuasion strategies in conversational text. The ablation in Section~\ref{sec:ablation} provides evidence for this distinction: scrambled strategy labels yield OOD performance within 1 percentage point of correct labels, suggesting that exposure to persuasion-domain text during fine-tuning, rather than accurate strategy supervision, is the primary mechanism. Ongoing control experiments (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}) will test whether fine-tuning on non-persuasion auxiliary tasks (e.g., sentiment classification or masked language modeling on the same data) produces comparable transfer, isolating whether the gains are attributable to persuasion-specific pragmatic features or to domain adaptation more broadly.
29	
30	\subsection{Dataset Artifacts and Adaptive Attacks}
31	
32	Machine learning classifiers are susceptible to dataset artifacts: spurious correlations between surface features and labels that inflate performance without genuine understanding~\citep{gururangan2018artifacts,niven2019probing,poliak2018hypothesis}. Debiasing methods~\citep{schuster2019debiasing} mitigate this by training against known artifacts, but the problem persists for safety-critical applications where attackers actively adapt. \citet{nasr2025attackermovessecond} demonstrate that BERT-based safety classifiers can be bypassed by adaptive adversaries who optimize against the classifier's decision boundary, and \citet{andriushchenko2024adaptive} show similar vulnerabilities in broader evaluation contexts. Red-teaming methodologies~\citep{perez2022redteaming,ganguli2022redteaming} and systematic attack benchmarks~\citep{mazeika2024harmbench} provide structured evaluation protocols but do not solve the underlying robustness problem.
33	
34	We acknowledge an important empirical observation: TF-IDF achieves F1 = 0.944 on our OOD evaluation, indicating inherent lexical separability between attack and benign conversations in current datasets. DisPeD's contribution over bag-of-words methods is not higher accuracy on static benchmarks but robustness under adversarial perturbation (0 percentage point degradation vs. 1.3 percentage points for TF-IDF and 11.8 percentage points for vanilla DeBERTa) and interpretable detection through persuasion strategy trajectories. Adaptive attacks that specifically target persuasion-level features represent an open challenge for future work.

% experiments.tex — D019 Reframe: Domain Exposure as Mechanism
% Requires: booktabs, multirow, graphicx, multicolumn (standard)

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Datasets.}
We train on 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak conversations and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, both generated via Qwen3-8B.
Topic anchoring ensures that benign conversations cover the same subject domains as jailbreak conversations and controls for topical confounds.
For out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, we generate 80 Foot-in-the-Door (FITD)~\citep{fitd2024} and 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} conversations through a separate pipeline with no overlap in attack templates or strategies with the training data.
The in-distribution (IID) test set consists of 76 held-out Crescendo conversations (38 jailbreak, 38 benign).
To assess adversarial robustness, we paraphrase the IID test set to produce 76 perturbed samples with mean BERTScore of 0.92 and lexical overlap of 0.20.

\paragraph{Model variants.}
We evaluate five variants that share the same Stage-2 pipeline (BiGRU aggregation over DeBERTa [CLS] embeddings, two-layer MLP classifier) and differ only in how the Stage-1 encoder is trained.
\textbf{9-class} (full model): DeBERTa-v3-base~\citep{he2021deberta} fine-tuned with a multi-task objective combining 9-class persuasion strategy classification and binary jailbreak-intent classification (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
\textbf{Binary}: the 9-class taxonomy collapsed to persuasion-present vs.\ absent, with the same multi-task setup.
\textbf{Scrambled}: the full 9-class setup with randomly permuted strategy labels.
\textbf{MLM}: continued pretraining with 15\% token masking on the same training conversations, without any classification heads.
\textbf{Vanilla DeBERTa}: the unfine-tuned encoder (control).
We additionally compare against \textbf{TF-IDF LR} (logistic regression over TF-IDF features) and LLM-as-judge baselines (Section~\ref{sec:llm_judge}).
This design progressively strips components to isolate the mechanism: if 9-class $\approx$ binary $\approx$ scrambled, label quality is non-essential; if MLM $\approx$ classification variants, supervised classification itself is non-essential; the gap between any fine-tuned variant and vanilla isolates the contribution of domain exposure.

\paragraph{Metrics and implementation.}
We report F1 score for binary jailbreak detection at turn prefix lengths $K \in \{1, 2, 3, 5\}$ and on full conversations.
IID results for the 9-class and vanilla variants report the mean and standard deviation across three random seeds (42, 123, 456); MLM and other variants use seed 42.
Stage-1 fine-tuning uses a learning rate of $2 \times 10^{-5}$, batch size 16, and 4 epochs.

\label{sec:decomposition}

We designed five variants to systematically decompose what enables cross-attack generalization.
Table~\ref{tab:evidence_hierarchy} reports DD and IID F1 for each variant.

\paragraph{Classification supervision is non-essential.}
The MLM variant achieves DD-Full F1 = 1.000 without any classification labels.
This is the definitive test: if unsupervised continued pretraining on the training conversations suffices for OOD generalization, then the classification objective (whether 9-class, binary, or scrambled) cannot be the mechanism.
The evidence hierarchy is clear:
\begin{quote}
\small
vanilla (0.284) $\ll$ MLM (1.000) $=$ scrambled (0.990) $=$ binary (0.990) $=$ 9-class (1.000)
\end{quote}
Every variant that includes continued training on jailbreak conversation text achieves DD-Full F1 $\geq$ 0.990.
The 70+ percentage point gap lies entirely between vanilla and any form of continued training, not between MLM and classification variants.

\paragraph{Label quality and granularity are non-factors.}
Replacing the 9-class taxonomy with randomly scrambled labels reduces DD-Full F1 from 1.000 to 0.990, a gap of 1 percentage point.
Collapsing to binary yields the same 0.990.
Both remain far above vanilla (F1 = 0.284), a gap exceeding 70 percentage points.
These results confirm the domain-exposure interpretation~\citep{gururangan2020dontstop}: the encoder learns useful features from exposure to persuasion-domain text during continued training, regardless of whether the supervision signal is correct, coarse, or random.

\paragraph{Temporal modeling is unnecessary.}
Replacing BiGRU with orderless mean pooling yields DD-Full F1 = 1.000, matching the BiGRU default (Table~\ref{tab:evidence_hierarchy}).
The detection signal resides in individual turn representations rather than their sequential arrangement.
BiGRU is the default aggregator in all other experiments.

\paragraph{Loss weighting is insensitive.}
We evaluated $\alpha \in \{0, 0.3, 0.5, 2.0\}$ for the multi-task loss weight.
All values achieve IID-Full F1 = 1.000.
The $\alpha=0$ variant (persuasion strategy classification only, no intent head) confirms that the persuasion task alone suffices for in-distribution detection.

\paragraph{Ongoing controls.}
Two additional control experiments are in progress to further test the domain-exposure hypothesis.
A topic-classification control replaces the persuasion strategy head with an unrelated classification task on the same training text, testing whether any supervised task on in-domain text suffices.
A Wikipedia-domain MLM control applies continued pretraining on out-of-domain text rather than jailbreak conversations, testing whether the specific text domain matters or whether any continued pretraining is sufficient.

Frontier language models fail at multi-turn jailbreak detection even with full conversation context.
Table~\ref{tab:llm_judge} reports zero-shot performance for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3-8B on the IID Crescendo test set.

GPT-5.5 achieves precision of 1.0 at all turn prefixes but recall ranges from only 0.105 to 0.290, resulting in F1 of 0.191 at $K$=2 and 0.449 at $K$=5.
A substantial fraction of responses are unparseable: the rate increases from 30\% at $K$=2 to 47\% on full conversations.
The F1 values exclude unparseable responses and represent upper bounds.
Full-conversation F1 (0.383) is lower than $K$=5 F1 (0.449) because the unparseable rate grows with context length.
The high precision but low recall pattern suggests that GPT-5.5 is deceived by Crescendo's surface educational framing: the model correctly identifies jailbreaks when it commits to a classification, but the majority of attacks go undetected.

Qwen3-8B performs worse across all prefixes (F1 from 0.000 at $K$=2 to 0.100 on full conversations) and produces no unparseable responses.
The failure of both a frontier commercial model and an open-weight model confirms a fundamental limitation of content-level reasoning for this task.
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo,li2024mhj}, and each turn maintains surface-level coherence with an innocuous cover topic.
Domain-adaptive continued training captures pragmatic features at a fraction of the inference cost of a frontier LLM.

\label{sec:strategy}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/paper/fig3_strategy_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Persuasion strategy transition count matrices for three attack types, based on ground-truth intended strategy labels from the dataset generation pipeline. Crescendo exhibits broad coverage across all strategy categories, while FITD and DD concentrate transitions in smaller subsets. These trajectories are an interpretability contribution: the decomposition in Section~\ref{sec:decomposition} establishes that the taxonomy does not drive detection performance.}
\label{fig:strategy_heatmap}
\end{figure*}

Although the persuasion taxonomy does not contribute to detection performance (Section~\ref{sec:decomposition}), it provides interpretability that MLM-only models cannot offer.
Figure~\ref{fig:strategy_heatmap} shows transition count matrices based on ground-truth intended strategy labels for three attack types.

Crescendo conversations exhibit broad transition coverage across all strategy categories, with 1,818 total transitions.
The highest concentration appears in Role Assignment self-transitions (545), with substantial activity across Emotional Manipulation, Logical Reframing, and Authority Appeal transitions.
This diverse pattern reflects Crescendo's design: each turn draws from a wide repertoire of strategies while incrementally shifting toward more aggressive persuasion.

FITD conversations show a markedly sparser pattern with 541 transitions concentrated in 4 active source strategies.
Role$\to$Obfuscation (161) is the dominant transition, consistent with FITD's structure of securing initial compliance through role assignment before obscuring the escalation path.

DD conversations span 5 active source strategies across 565 transitions.
Emotion$\to$Obfuscation (129) is the dominant transition, consistent with DD's hybrid design of embedding harmful content within emotionally engaging and distracting contexts~\citep{deceptivedelight2024}.

These trajectory signatures allow security analysts to inspect why a conversation was flagged.
Different attack types produce recognizable strategy fingerprints.
This interpretability is the taxonomy's sole contribution after the MLM control result: it does not improve detection, but it makes detection decisions human-readable.
The decomposition in Section~\ref{sec:decomposition} confirms this directly: replacing BiGRU with mean pooling (which discards turn order) yields identical detection performance, so the model detects persuasion presence per turn rather than temporal trajectory patterns.
